source: Morewedge, Yoon, Scopelliti, Symborski, Korris, Kassam (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Two IARPA-funded experiments compared a serious computer game (feedback, personalised after-action reviews, practice) with a passive instructional video. Both cut bias right after training and months later. The game was stronger on most comparisons right after training.
numbers: Exp1 (N=278 recruited; 243 lab, 196 follow-up at 8 weeks): overall bias d pre-post game 1.68, video 0.69; pre-follow-up game 1.11, video 0.66. Exp2 (N=269; 238 lab, 192 follow-up at 12 weeks): overall d game 1.74/1.16, video 1.75/1.07. Abstract: games -31.94% immediate, -23.57% later; videos -18.60% and -19.20%.
quote: Games, which provided personalized feedback and practice, produced larger effects than did videos.
limits: Convenience sample in Pittsburgh; bias scales built by the authors, some with weak reliability (anchoring alpha .52-.62); one-shot, no repetition; follow-up attrition 20-25%; the authors also made the games, scoring was checked by a third party.
agent_relevance: Feedback plus practice beats instruction alone, as the guardrail design expects. A stored lesson library for an LLM should hold worked feedback, not only warnings.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Exp1 per-bias breakdown
finding: In Exp1 the game beat the video for bias blind spot, fundamental attribution error and confirmation bias, at both time points. Confirmation bias decayed most at follow-up.
numbers: Pre-post d (game/video): blind spot .98/.49; FAE 1.12/.38; confirmation 1.09/.38. Pre-follow-up d: blind spot .89/.49; FAE .72/.52; confirmation .58/.26. Game vs video at follow-up: confirmation F(1,193)=5.17, p<.05; FAE F=6.53, p<.05.
limits: Per-bias decay is uneven: confirmation bias effect roughly halved in the game group over 8 weeks.
agent_relevance: Confirmation-style errors need repeated refresh. An agent scaffold should re-inject the lesson each run rather than assume it persists.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Exp2 per-bias breakdown and adaptive practice
finding: In Exp2 anchoring, projection and representativeness fell. Video equalled the game for anchoring and (at follow-up) representativeness, but the game was better for projection. Exp2 added adaptive practice: wrong practice answers triggered extra items with feedback (up to 16).
numbers: Pre-post d (game/video): anchoring .70/.80; projection 1.11/.49; representativeness 1.51/1.80. Pre-follow-up d: anchoring .63/.66; projection .54/.14; representativeness 1.05/1.09. Game vs video at 12 weeks overall: F(1,189)=3.66, p=.057.
limits: Video reached parity on rule-like biases (anchoring, representativeness). The edge for games appears where a biased intuition must be noticed in oneself (projection).
agent_relevance: Feedback matters most for biases that are invisible to the self. Rule-like biases may be fixed by a short reminder.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) transfer to untrained facets and bias knowledge
finding: Debiasing generalised to confirmation-bias facets the game never taught. Bias knowledge (recognising biases) rose more for the video, yet the video did not debias more, so knowing is not the same as being less biased.
numbers: Confirmation bias, trained facets: posttest d=.78, follow-up d=.24. Untrained facets: posttest d=.79, follow-up d=.65. Bias knowledge Exp1 game 35.78 -> 58.54 -> 47.98; video 35.29 -> 69.28 -> 50.63.
limits: Untrained facets were in the same bias family and the same game story. Not proof of transfer to distant tasks.
agent_relevance: Teaching the principle (hold variables constant, test the disconfirming case) transfers inside a family. Test our scaffold on held-out variants.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training improves decision making in the field (accepted manuscript)
finding: Field test of transfer. Graduate business students were trained with the one-shot game, and by natural schedule some solved an unannounced Challenger-style business case after training and some before. Trained students more often rejected the confirming, reckless option.
numbers: N=290 (trained 182, untrained 108). Chose to race: 58.8% trained vs 72.2% untrained, b=-.60, exp(b)=.549, 95% CI [.33,.92], p=.022; abstract states 29% less likely. Mean gap between training and case 17.96 days (SD 19.86). In 2-day window (n=50) 50.0% vs 85.7%.
quote: Trained participants were 29% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming solution than untrained participants.
limits: Quasi-random assignment by schedule, not a true RCT; single case; completion differed (73.1% vs 63.0%, p=.071). Authors flag one field experiment.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that a one-shot lesson carries into a new, unflagged decision. Supports lesson plus practice fed into context for an agent.

source: Sellier et al. (2019) mechanism and delay
finding: Training worked through less confirmatory argument, not through more confidence. The effect did not fade across a 43-52 day gap. Trained students were less confident in their choice.
numbers: Trained students wrote fewer confirming arguments: 1.45 vs 2.07, d=.39, p=.001; disconfirming arguments 1.23 vs 1.08, n.s. (p=.377). Short vs long lag: 56.8% vs 63.2% chose race, 95% CI diff [-2.07%, 9.10%], p=.419 (n=182). Confidence lower after training: b=-.43, p=.017.
limits: Long-lag group was only 31.3% of the trained group (about 57 people), so no strong claim on decay. Disconfirming arguments did not rise, only confirming ones fell.
agent_relevance: The lever is cutting one-sided search, not adding doubt. In a scaffold, a disconfirm-before-commit step is the matching operator.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Across four years of the IARPA forecasting tournament, short training (under an hour; probabilistic reasoning and scenario modules) consistently improved Brier accuracy. Part of the gain ran through practice.
numbers: Year1: probability-trained n=119, scenario-trained n=113 vs control n=152, +10% and +11% Brier improvement. Year2: trained n=205 vs n=194, t(395)=5.95, p<.001, 12%. Year3: n=97 vs 116, t(207)=2.32, p=.021, 6%. Year4: n=131 vs 102, t(225)=2.20, p=.028, 7%. Indirect effect via practice -0.02, CI [-0.04,-0.01].
quote: it consistently improved accuracy (Brier scores) by 6 to 11% over the control condition.
limits: Volunteer forecasters (about 83% male, mean age 41, many graduate-educated); effect shrank from 12% to 6-7% in later years; training bundles several tips (CHAMPS KNOW).
agent_relevance: Mnemonic principles plus practice with outcome feedback improve judgment. Matches schema ideas of base-rate and scenario steps backed by a score loop.

source: Larrick, Morgan, Nisbett (1990) Teaching the use of cost-benefit reasoning in everyday life
finding: Brief training on sunk-cost and opportunity-cost rules changed answers on questions in new content, and formally trained faculty used the rules more. A phone follow-up found some self-reported behaviour change.
numbers: Study 2: trained subjects chose the normative answer for themselves on 44% of problems vs 28.6% untrained, t(87)=4.77, p<.01; trap answer 30.1% vs 38.6%, p<.05. Training x problem interaction F(3,261)=122.18, p<.001. Follow-up: 40 trained, 40 untrained, nine-item index showed more sunk-cost ignoring; another index t(78)=1.64, p=.10.
limits: Self-reported behaviour, not observed; half-hour lab training, short follow-up; behavioural effects mostly marginal. Strong content similarity between trained and test problems.
agent_relevance: Teach a rule, then test on new content in the same family. Early support that a rule given in context can be applied in new tasks.

source: Aczel, Bago, Szollosi, Foldes, Lukacs (2015) Is it time for studying real-life debiasing? Analogical intervention
finding: Analogical-encoding training for 10 biases, compared with awareness training and no training, tested 4 weeks later. Only statistical-principle biases improved. Awareness training alone did not help the other biases.
numbers: N=154; 10 biases tested before and 4 weeks after (covariation detection, sample-size insensitivity, base-rate neglect, regression to the mean, outcome bias, sunk cost, framing, anchoring, overconfidence, planning fallacy). Gains concentrated in statistical tasks, strongest for insensitivity to sample size.
limits: Non-statistical biases showed nothing for either training. Small groups per condition; the authors call it exploratory.
agent_relevance: Warnings (awareness) did not work here; analogies for abstract rules did. A scaffold should give worked analogies, not just 'beware bias X'.

source: O'Sullivan, Schofield (2019) A cognitive forcing tool to mitigate cognitive bias: a randomised controlled trial
finding: A null result. An online cognitive-forcing tool did not lower diagnostic error on bias-inducing vignettes, though doctors liked it.
numbers: N=76 doctors (student to attending). Mean cases correct 2.8 (tool) vs 3.1 (control), 95% CI -0.94 to 0.45, p=0.49. Think-aloud with 20 doctors was positive.
limits: Small volunteer sample; vignette task; single session. Underpowered for small effects.
agent_relevance: A checklist that feels useful may do nothing. Our loop must measure effects on held-out items, not trust self-reports of rigour.

source: Cognitive forcing and need for cognition in AI-assisted decision making (Sci Rep, 2025/2026)
finding: Cognitive-forcing interventions (delay AI advice or slow the decision) did not stop people following biased AI advice on violence-risk vignettes. High need for cognition did help.
numbers: Exp1 n=281, Exp2 n=373. Biased AI advice produced biased decisions in both; three CF interventions did not reduce it; high-NFC participants were less biased.
limits: Vignettes with stereotype content; online samples; measures following of AI advice, not own errors.
agent_relevance: Slowing down is not enough. A forced pause in an agent loop needs a specific check, not just delay.

source: National risk analysts study (2025) Debiasing training reduces confirmation bias in national risk analysts (Sci Rep)
finding: A one-shot debiasing session (15-min lecture on biases, then the Carter Racing case) cut confirmation bias for both real analysts and master's students. Analysts were less biased to begin with.
numbers: Analysts N=71 (over half of a national population), students N=118. Training main effect F(1,169)=20.744, p<.001, partial eta2=.109; group effect F(1,169)=25.928, partial eta2=.133. ANCOVA pre vs post: general F(1,168)=104.58, eta2p=.384; risk F(1,168)=46.0, eta2p=.215. No group x training interaction (all F<1). Blind spot also fell: F(1,163)=5.72, p=.018, eta2p=.034.
limits: Immediate post-test only, no delay test; scales adapted from earlier work; expertise lowered bias, contrary to common claims.
agent_relevance: An extension of the Morewedge/Sellier work to experts. Expertise did not remove the need for training.

source: Ludolph, Schulz (2018) Debiasing health-related judgments and decision making: a systematic review (Med Decis Making)
finding: Systematic review of debiasing in health. Most interventions were at least partly successful, but transfer to real settings and conceptual rigour are weak.
numbers: From search snippet only: 68 articles, 87 studies; majority of interventions (n=60) at least partially successful; targets were optimistic bias (n=25), framing (n=14), base-rate neglect (n=10).
limits: Not opened; counts come from a search abstract and two versions disagree. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Gives the base rate for success in the literature: most work, few are tested for transfer.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Tested prompt-based debiasing on LLM admissions decisions (anchoring, framing, status quo, group attribution, primacy). Self-help (the model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias cues) worked best. Awareness reminders were inconsistent, and few-shot and contrastive examples often broke the model.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B and 13B. GPT-4 framing gap admit-vs-reject: baseline -0.405; awareness -0.470, contrastive -0.410, counterfactual -0.570, self-help -0.010. GPT-3.5 framing baseline +0.165, self-help -0.080. Llama-2-7B contrastive: 0.996 admit / 1.000 reject (collapse). Self-help left 0% framing-biased prompt parts in Llama-2-13B.
limits: Admissions scenario only; open models old (Llama-2); 400-prompt subsets for cost; some cells flagged as instruction failure.
agent_relevance: Awareness hints can make some LLMs worse, as warnings did in humans. Rewriting the problem to remove the bias cue is the strongest option here.

source: Sumita, Takeuchi, Kashima (2024) Cognitive biases in LLMs: a survey and mitigation experiments
finding: Two crowdsourcing debiasing methods were tried on LLMs. The social projection (SoPro) prompt, which helps humans, did little or hurt. A bias-awareness reminder (AwaRe) helped.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, six biases. Bandwagon score GPT-3.5: with-reason .524, SoPro .955 (worse), AwaRe .260. GPT-4: baseline .214, SoPro .255, AwaRe .142. AwaRe helped GPT-3.5 on order, compassion fade, egocentric, bandwagon, attentional bias; on GPT-4 only bandwagon and verbosity.
limits: Two models, one prompt wording each, no weights changed; AwaRe needs the bias named per task.
agent_relevance: The human projection trick did not transfer to LLMs, so each human technique needs an LLM test. Awareness helped here but hurt in BiasBuster; effect depends on model.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLMs with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring appears in all tested LLMs and is shallow (acts in early layers). Standard fixes did little; explicit reasoning helped most.
numbers: 22% to 61% of questions anchored across models; reasoning models lowest. Llama-3.1-8B total anchored 34.7% baseline; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse); self-improving 38.4%; adversarial fine-tune 33.3%; Anti-Dual-Process two-phase prompt 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B: baseline 40.0%; self-improving 48.0% (worse); Anti-DP 40.8%. Best gain about 10 points.
limits: Two small instruction models for mitigation; Anti-DP did not help numerical questions on Qwen; table alignment partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: A 'think carefully' prompt did not help; a structured two-phase standard-then-answer step did on one model. Supports a thinking schema over a bare warning.

source: Lyu, Ren, Feng, Wang, Chen, Ren, de Rijke (2025) Self-adaptive cognitive debiasing (SACD) for LLMs in decision-making
finding: Loop of detect bias, analyse it, rewrite the prompt, repeat. It beat CoT, Reflexion, debate, zero-shot, few-shot and self-help debiasing, also with several biases at once. Few-shot debiasing and debate often made things worse.
numbers: FOMC finance task, mean bias score (lower is better): Llama-3.1-8B vanilla .3805 -> SACD .1570 (self-help .2100, CoT .3425, debate .5020). Llama-70B .1648 -> .1080. GPT-3.5 .4765 -> .1175. GPT-4o .3650 -> .0300 (self-help .0625, few-shot debiasing .7350). GPT-3.5 multi-bias .9540 -> .1220. Scores fall across iterations (0.2070, 0.1460, 0.1175 on one setting).
limits: Bias is detected by the same LLM being debiased; scores are on constructed prompts with one injected bias type each; also run on healthcare and legal tasks.
agent_relevance: Closest analogue to feedback plus practice in prompts: iterative detect-and-fix beats one-pass warnings. Template for a scaffold operator.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak, An (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Biases fall in four families. Prompt-level debiasing fixed Response biases but backfired on Judgment biases. Activation steering cut bias by about a third.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B. Prompt debiasing: Response +40.5% position independence; Judgment -4.4% accuracy (backfire); Info Processing -1.1%; Social +5.9%. Probe accuracy 99.8% (Judgment), 98.2%, 99.2%, 93.9% (Social); cross-model probe 49.7%. Steering: 26-32% bias score reduction; Qwen up to -19.0pp capability for Judgment biases. Cross-model steering rate r(246)=.621.
limits: Steering needs open weights; bias defined by computable ground truth, a narrower notion than human heuristics research.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as humans: general warnings help superficial biases and may hurt judgment biases. Argues for per-bias tests of any guardrail.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Making bias non-predictive: Epistemic Independence Training (EIT) via RL
finding: Training an LLM with RL where a bias cue (bandwagon claim) is right half the time and wrong half the time taught it to ignore the cue, and transferred to unseen cue types. Prompt mitigation and plain SFT did not generalise.
numbers: Qwen3-4B trained on bandwagon only: adversarial-bias accuracy 70.1% -> 83.3% (+13.2), robustness +16.4, unseen distraction robustness +39.1. Qwen3-1.7B: SFT cut clean accuracy 0.843 -> 0.521, EIT kept 0.851.
limits: Small models; MMLU-Pro style items; weight training, which our scaffold cannot use directly.
agent_relevance: Mirrors feedback plus practice: a cue that is non-predictive of reward gets ignored. An agent score loop should include conflicting-cue cases.

source: He, Liu (2025) Investigating the impact of LLM personality on cognitive bias manifestation
finding: Persona prompts change how biased an LLM is and how much an awareness prompt helps. Conscientiousness and agreeableness personas tended to respond better to debiasing, but not in every model.
numbers: Six prevalent biases found; sunk cost and group attribution had minimal effect. Awareness mitigation sometimes increased bias; in GPT-4o conscientiousness failed to help. Llama3-70B baseline bias 91.23% in one test; GPT-4 low baseline (4.7%).
limits: Persona effects are model-specific; effects mixed and several small.
agent_relevance: A single debiasing prompt will not behave the same across models or personas. Calibrate guardrails per model.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned LMs exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF introduce or amplify decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias relative to the base model.
numbers: Compared GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families before and after tuning. Biases stronger in Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. (I read the abstract, setup and framing; per-model tables not extracted.)
limits: Template-generated tasks; no human control in the same format.
agent_relevance: Training for helpfulness can add bias. A scaffold sits above the tuned model and can check it.

source: Liu, He (2024) The decoy dilemma in online medical information evaluation
finding: A crowd experiment and an LLM replica showed decoy effects in both humans and LLMs, more often in the LLMs. Larger, newer models separated credible from false information better but were more swayed by a salient decoy misinformation item.
numbers: Between-subject crowd study plus LLM simulation on COVID-19 medical credibility ratings; abstract states the decoy effect was more prevalent in LLM judgments.
limits: Read the abstract and setup; effect sizes not extracted. IR credibility task only.
agent_relevance: Bigger models are not free of context bias; guardrails against option-set effects stay useful.

source: Binz, Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat humans on many vignette tasks but small perturbations to the vignettes sent it far off. It failed a causal reasoning task.
numbers: Battery of canonical experiments in decision making, information search, deliberation and causal reasoning (abstract-level reading).
limits: Old model (GPT-3); not a measure of current models.
agent_relevance: Wording brittleness: a debiasing result in one phrasing may not hold in another, so test several phrasings.

source: Raj, Mansouri, Caliskan, Anastasopoulos, Zhu (2026) Debias It Yourself: teaching LLMs cognitive bias-mitigation interventions
finding: Five human social-psychology interventions (recognise, imagine counter-examples, reinforce, etc.) turned into LLM procedures via in-context examples, instruction tuning, and guided self-revision. Revision alone and train-plus-revise ranked best.
numbers: Three models (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3.5-27B), five bias benchmarks, eleven baselines, three reasoning benchmarks. Mean bias as low as 2% at 90% reasoning accuracy; reduction up to 14.8% on unseen bias dimensions.
limits: Social stereotype benchmarks (BBQ, StereoSet, WinoBias), not judgment biases like anchoring.
agent_relevance: Guided self-revision (recognise, then imagine the alternative) is the LLM form of consider-the-opposite and needs no weight change.

source: Fong, Krantz, Nisbett (1986) and Nisbett, Fong, Lehman, Cheng (1987) Teaching reasoning (as described in Morewedge 2015 and Sellier 2019)
finding: Statistical-reasoning courses and graduate training in probabilistic sciences raise use of statistics and logic on everyday problems. Short training often fails to generalise unless extensive or unless people know they are being tested.
numbers: No numbers extracted: originals not opened. Secondary statements only.
limits: Second-hand; original effect sizes need checking.
agent_relevance: Large doses work, short doses are fragile; treat the scaffold as a permanent dose, not a one-off hint.

source: Fischhoff (1982) Debiasing; Hirt, Markman (1995) consider-an-alternative (as described in Morewedge 2015)
finding: Fischhoff's four training steps (name the bias, give its direction, feedback, extended feedback with coaching) frame the game vs video contrast. Consider-an-alternative strategies are named as the most promising rule-based training.
numbers: No numbers extracted; Morewedge 2015 maps its game to all four Fischhoff steps and the video to steps 1, 2 and strategies without feedback.
limits: Second-hand. Originals unopened.
agent_relevance: A ready checklist for lesson design: name, direction, feedback, coached practice.

source: Arkes (1991); Milkman, Chugh, Bazerman (2009); Kahneman and Egan (2011) (skeptics, as cited in Sellier 2019)
finding: Skeptical position: training teaches people to spot and fix bias when prompted but does not transfer where no reminder exists, may be a Hawthorne effect, and can interfere with useful heuristics. Sellier 2019 was built to test exactly this.
numbers: No numbers; positions as summarised by Sellier et al.
limits: Second-hand summary of skeptics.
agent_relevance: The skeptical case is the reason for held-out, unannounced tests of our agent.

source: Sedlmeier, Gigerenzer (2001) Teaching Bayesian reasoning in less than two hours
finding: Training on building frequency representations beat training on the Bayes rule for immediate learning and stability over time, while rule training transferred about as well.
numbers: From a search snippet only; no effect sizes extracted.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Representation (natural frequencies) is a cheap scaffold for statistical tasks.

source: Anesthesiology trainees consider-the-opposite trial (2025, title only)
finding: Europe PMC listing: consider-the-opposite debiasing to improve self-assessment accuracy in anesthesiology trainees. Not opened.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Title only; result unknown.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a later read on consider-the-opposite in professionals.

source: Schwarz et al. (2002) When debiasing backfires: accessible content and accessibility experiences in debiasing hindsight (title only)
finding: Title in Europe PMC listing. Known idea from this line: asking for many reasons can feel hard and backfire. Not opened, mechanism unverified here.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Possible boundary on how many counter-arguments to demand from an agent.
